intro: The finale combines a returning rondo tune with fugal entries and transformed Adagietto material. The brass chorale glimpsed in the second movement returns near the end in D major. The complete source includes a probable non-musical tail after the apparent close.
question: How does a returning tune remain distinct when other themes sound alongside it?

sections.label: Introduction · instrumental conversation
sections.mNote: horn and woodwinds exchange short introductory ideas

sections.label: Rondo theme and first fugato

sections.mNote: familiar ideas change context, register and accompaniment

sections.label: Further returns and contrapuntal growth
sections.mNote: returning themes alternate with renewed imitative activity

cues.title: A held note becomes conversation
cues.text: The opening horn holds an A, the pitch with which the preceding Adagietto ends. Short bassoon, oboe and clarinet phrases then assemble the finale’s material conversationally, before the main movement gathers its pace.
cues.evidence: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 183, shows the horn A and introductory wind phrases; the link to the Adagietto is described by Lew Smoley. The report shows a sparse, quiet 0:00–0:40 region. This does not claim gapless playback between separate files.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Fragments become a rondo tune
cues.text: The introductory exchanges lead to a more continuous, horn-led tune. In a rondo, recognisable returning material provides orientation; here its later appearances will have to share the texture with other active lines.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 183 marks Allegro commodo for the main theme after the introduction. The report rises from −39.7 dB at 0:40 to −22.3 at 0:50, supporting an approximate 0:46 join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A fugato starts underneath
cues.text: Cellos begin the running fugato before the preceding phrase has fully released its hold. Listen for successive parts joining the idea while earlier voices continue: the texture grows by overlap, not by a series of isolated solos.
cues.evidence: Peters pp. 185–186 show the cello entry and subsequent string entries; Smoley describes the overlap. The report’s activity increases through 1:15–1:45. This is a broad passage anchor, not an exact cello attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Fifth’s second summer
cues.text: Mahler completes the symphony’s composition in the summer of 1902, after work during the previous summer. The score will continue changing in later revisions, especially in its orchestral detail.
cues.evidence: Composition: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. Revisions: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A tune survives its accompaniment
cues.text: The returning rondo material can remain clear even when its accompaniment changes. Try keeping the tune’s rhythmic outline in mind while listening to the smaller moving notes around it.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s finale guide traces the rondo theme’s returns among fugal episodes: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-5-rondo-finale-allegro-allegro-giocoso-frisch/. The report has a quieter 2:35–2:45 region followed by renewed weight at 2:50–3:10; no exact return is aligned.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The Adagietto has another pace
cues.text: The finale reworks material from the Adagietto at a quicker pace. Listen for a lyrical shape that seems to belong to the preceding movement, rather than expecting its old string-and-harp texture or its slow tempo to return unchanged.
cues.evidence: The score and Smoley’s guide establish the transformed Adagietto material. The report’s changing 3:15–4:25 region supplies only a broad placement; no particular melodic quotation is asserted at 3:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Motion changes its scale
cues.text: The first large span allows its activity to thin out before the next gathering. Listen for how a quieter texture exposes the shape of a phrase that was less obvious in the denser writing.
cues.evidence: The report marks strong changes at 4:22, 4:30 and 4:42. Relative level falls from −17.8 dB at 4:25 to −34.3 at 4:35, remaining lower through 5:05.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Returning does not mean restarting
cues.text: Mahler combines rondo returns with developmental work on the themes. A familiar fragment may appear in another register or alongside a different line, so recognition need not signal a return to the opening’s complete arrangement.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the finale’s combination of rondo and sonata-like processes. The 4:30–4:52 report boundaries locate a broad change of texture; this is not a bar-exact claim about the start of a formal development.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Follow an entry beyond its beginning
cues.text: When a running figure enters, stay with it as another part joins. That continuing line is what makes the passage contrapuntal; hearing only each new entrance can conceal the independence of the parts.
cues.evidence: The score’s fugato technique and Smoley’s account support the listening task. The report records increased activity and level through 5:10–5:45, without separating instruments or counting written entries.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Counterpoint is not a Bach quotation
cues.text: Mahler’s interest in Bach helps place the finale’s imitative writing in context. Fugue-like entries are a technique, however, not evidence that this movement quotes a particular Bach theme.
cues.evidence: The Bach connection is discussed at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. No specific borrowed melody is asserted.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A crest opens into lighter writing
cues.text: This active span gathers weight, then pulls back. Listen for the change of balance after the crest: a continuing line can become easier to hear when the surrounding orchestral mass decreases.
cues.evidence: The report rises to −11.7 dB at 6:40, then falls to −21.8 at 6:50; boundaries at 6:44 and 6:50 support the broad turning region.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Longer lines among the fragments
cues.text: Alongside the short returning figures, the finale makes room for more sustained melodic writing. Listen for the distinction between a lyrical line and the smaller motives that accompany or interrupt it.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 210 shows a layered lyrical passage with horn and string lines; Smoley traces the contrast with fugato material. The report’s less densely active 6:50–7:35 span is a provisional regional anchor, not a p. 210 bar alignment.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The texture gathers again
cues.text: The next span rebuilds from a lighter starting point. The finale keeps alternating ways of presenting its material: a tune in the foreground, several independent lines, or short gestures passed around the orchestra.
cues.evidence: The report marks 7:46, followed by increasing activity and level from 8:00 through 8:50. The score and guide establish the alternating thematic textures; no exact return family is assigned to the section marker.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A crest is not an ending
cues.text: A powerful crest does not yet end the finale. Hear the following continuation as part of the design: Mahler reserves the cross-movement chorale for a later, broader statement.
cues.evidence: 8:50 is among the report’s loudest windows; substantial pitched material continues afterwards. Peters p. 244 establishes the later chorale, without placing it at this earlier crest.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A tune among independent lines
cues.text: Listen for a prominent melodic outline while the surrounding parts keep their own motion. Doubling a melody adds weight; counterpoint adds another line with its own contour. The finale uses both resources.
cues.evidence: The finale score and Smoley’s guide distinguish homophonic returns from fugato textures. The report shows continued activity through 9:00–9:35; this listening task does not identify a particular doubling at 9:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: D major at the far end
cues.text: The Fifth opens in C♯ minor but ends in D major. That large-scale change is one reason a single key label tells only part of the symphony’s story; the finale’s tonal goal is not the opening march’s home key.
cues.evidence: The opening and final keys are established by the score and discussed at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. This cue makes a whole-work statement, not a local-key claim at 10:00.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The strongest measured crest recedes
cues.text: The recording reaches its strongest measured orchestral swell, then loses weight quickly. Listen across that retreat: the quieter continuation is not the end of the file or the end of the musical argument.
cues.evidence: 10:25 is the loudest five-second window at −4.4 dB. The report falls to −23.3 at 10:35 and −32.8 at 10:45, with boundaries at 10:36 and 10:52.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Rebuilding from reduced forces
cues.text: After the withdrawal, follow how a phrase acquires support again. Mahler can restore momentum through a succession of small additions rather than asking the whole orchestra to return at once.
cues.evidence: The guide describes the late rebuilding and thematic combinations. The report shows low-level 10:40–11:25 windows, then rising level and activity through 11:35–12:05; instrumental additions are not individually timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Keep the earlier chorale in mind
cues.text: Recall the broad brass statement in the second movement, where it did not secure the ending. The finale’s last large arrival will bring that material back in a different structural position, near the end of the whole symphony.
cues.evidence: The cross-movement chorale return is documented in the finale score, p. 244, and Smoley’s guide. This is an anticipatory comparison, not a claim that the chorale enters at 12:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The final gathering gains weight
cues.text: The later buildup becomes more forceful without first clearing the texture. Listen for an approaching broad statement above the motion already under way.
cues.evidence: The report marks changes at 12:20, 12:30 and 12:38, then rises through 12:35–13:05. The score supplies the approaching chorale identity; the report supplies only the growth contour.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The chorale returns in the finale
cues.text: The brass chorale from the second movement returns in D major, with quick string motion beneath its broader values. What previously proved temporary now belongs to the symphony’s final stretch, though the music still has a closing rush to make.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 244, Pesante, shows the broad brass chorale over running strings; the guide establishes its relation to movement II. Strong 13:00–13:30 windows and D-major support at 13:20–13:30 locate the passage approximately, not its first chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quick punctuation, not a fade
cues.text: The score follows the broad chorale with a faster coda and a Presto ending of short, accented orchestral gestures. Listen for that musical punctuation separately from whatever the recording retains after it.
cues.evidence: Peters pp. 248 and 251 show the faster closing writing, Presto and secco attacks. The report remains strongly tonal through the 13:55–14:15 region, then changes sharply in spectral character. The exact final note is not established.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A probable non-musical tail
cues.text: The complete source continues beyond the apparent musical close. Its later sound is probably audience noise, but that identification and the exact cutoff remain unconfirmed. No further orchestral events are assigned to this part of the file.
cues.evidence: Brightness rises sharply at 14:20–14:30, with weak tonal correlations across much of 14:30–17:05. This supports a provisional recorded-tail boundary at 14:25, not a confirmed applause identification or measured final chord.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The work’s first public performance
cues.text: While the source tail continues, a historical point: Mahler conducts the Fifth’s premiere in Cologne on 18 October 1904. The score heard here belongs to a later performance whose date and venue have not been established.
cues.evidence: Premiere: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/. Commons and Archive give an addition date, not a documented session date. No musical event is claimed in the probable tail.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A piano roll, not this orchestra
cues.text: Mahler records a piano roll of the first movement in Leipzig in 1905. It preserves a different kind of performance document; it is not an orchestral recording of the Fifth and is not the source of these Peabody files.
cues.evidence: The 9 November 1905 Welte-Mignon roll session is recorded at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/. This historical note sits in the probable non-musical source tail.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Compare the two chorale settings
cues.text: For another hearing, compare the second movement’s chorale with the finale’s. The melodic connection matters, but so do the aftermaths: one gives way to renewed fragments, while the other leads into the symphony’s final coda.
cues.evidence: The relation is established by Peters II p. 102 and V p. 244 and by Smoley’s guides. This is a retrospective listening suggestion during the probable recorded tail, not a claim that music is still playing at 16:40.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

transitions.title: Scattered exchanges become a continuous theme
transitions.how: The opening horn A and short woodwind phrases assemble material that the main tempo can turn into a continuous tune. With Allegro commodo, the horn-led theme acquires steadier accompaniment and a clearer D-major frame. Shortly afterwards, a cello fugato enters before the preceding phrase has entirely finished: overlap, rather than a full stop, carries the music into independent running lines.
transitions.evidence: Peters pp. 183, 185–186 document the main-theme tempo and overlapping cello entry. The rise at 0:45–0:50 anchors the main-theme join; increased activity at 1:15–1:45 supports the following fugato. The marker does not time both events as one attack.

transitions.title: The full texture leaves room for fragments
transitions.how: The first large span yields to a quieter texture in which shorter ideas can be heard separately. Mahler continues working with the rondo and fugato material, changing register, accompaniment and the combinations of parts. The reduced orchestral weight makes room for a new gathering of independent lines instead of sealing off the preceding music with a final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the continuing transformations. The report’s strong 4:22, 4:30 and 4:42 boundaries and level fall at 4:30–4:35 locate the broad texture change; a specific cadence or modulation is not claimed.

transitions.title: Lighter writing feeds another accumulation
transitions.how: A lighter continuation gives way to renewed rhythmic activity. Returning melodic outlines and running figures occupy the same larger span, so the join works by regrouping familiar material rather than replacing it with a wholly new theme. As the parts accumulate, the orchestra recovers weight without abandoning the independence of its lines.
transitions.evidence: The guide establishes the recurrent thematic and fugal processes. The 7:46 boundary, low 7:40–7:55 windows and rising activity through 8:05–8:50 support a broad 7:46 turning region; no exact thematic entry is asserted.

transitions.title: The crest breaks into a quieter continuation
transitions.how: The large buildup loses orchestral weight sharply, exposing a thinner continuation. That retreat leaves space for the later gathering: brief figures and longer lines regain support in stages rather than immediately restoring the previous tutti. The apparent interruption therefore becomes part of the preparation for the ending.
transitions.evidence: The 10:25 maximum is followed by the 10:36 boundary and a rapid fall through 10:35–10:45; another strong boundary follows at 10:52. The movement guide supplies the late rebuilding context, not an exact bar alignment.

transitions.title: The earlier chorale gains a final setting
transitions.how: The gathering music reaches the D-major brass chorale already heard in the second movement. Mahler marks the broad statement Pesante and keeps fast string figures beneath it, so the arrival combines sustained chords with continuing motion. Instead of dissolving as it did earlier in the symphony, this chorale leads onward to the faster coda and the short final gestures.
transitions.evidence: Peters pp. 244, 248 and 251 establish the chorale, subsequent acceleration and ending. The report’s rising 12:35–13:05 contour and strong 13:20–13:30 D-major region support a provisional 13:00 section anchor; the chorale’s exact first chord is unaligned.

transitions.title: The written ending and the retained file tail
transitions.how: The score ends with a Presto rush and short secco orchestral punctuation, not a composed fade. The selected file then appears to retain a predominantly non-musical tail, possibly audience sound. This marker distinguishes a probable recording boundary from a formal join in Mahler’s composition; neither the exact final chord nor the identity of the later sound has been confirmed by audition.
transitions.evidence: Peters p. 251 establishes the written ending. The report changes from strong tonal material near 14:00–14:15 to much higher brightness at 14:20–14:30 and weak tonal correlations afterwards. 14:25 is explicitly provisional, not an exact cutoff.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, V, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed pp. 183, 185–186, 210, 244, 248, 251. Broad scoring snapshots, not continuous entry tracking; the performance’s edition is unknown. No musical orchestration is assigned after the provisional 14:25 source-tail boundary.

timeline.note: Introduction, p. 183: sustained horn and short wind phrases appear successively, with a quiet violin note; not a simultaneous ensemble at the first instant.
Main-theme passage, p. 183, Allegro commodo: horn-led melody with supporting wind and bass parts; approximate placement at the 0:45–0:50 rise.
First fugato, pp. 185–186: cellos initiate the running line and further strings enter while other parts continue; individual entries are not timed.
Lyrical passage, p. 210: horn and string lines with sustained wind support; provisional placement within the lighter 6:50–7:35 region.
Final chorale, p. 244: broad brass chords above active strings; placement in the strong 13:00–13:30 region is approximate.
Closing pages, pp. 248–251: fast orchestral figures and short final punctuation; broad placement before the spectral change, not a measured final-note time.
Provisional recorded-tail region: no score-based instrumental events assigned. The sound may be audience noise; its identity and the exact musical cutoff are unconfirmed.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
